newsitem.title: SPAIN: Violence, fear mark strike called by Basque rebels.
newsitem.headline: Violence, fear mark strike called by Basque rebels.

text.p: Mounting tension in Spain's Basque country erupted into violence in San Sebastian on Friday where police clashed with some 2,000 supporters of a strike called by the political arm of separatist rebels ETA.

Basque police, angered by a jury's acquittal on Thursday of a man charged with killing two officers, said they were quick to the trigger when quelling a march by Herri Batasuna (HB) which called the strike to protest at the jailing of its leaders.

"I want to intervene (in the march). I'm here voluntarily," one policeman in riot gear and a ski mask to hide his identity told Reuters. "We've had enough. These thugs are terrorising the shopkeepers, forcing them to join the strike."
Protesters marching through the cobbled streets of the northern resort city pounded on windows and shouted for an end to repression as police kept an uneasy distance.
When the demonstration moved to the newer part of the city, police moved in, firing rubber bullets into the air and triggering a stampede of fleeing protesters.
HB supporters overturned rubbish bins to make barricades and smashed shop windows as they ran through the streets.

One of the victims, the owner of a clothing shop that had a window broken, just shrugged his shoulders when asked why he had defied the rebels' strike call by staying open. "It's a nuisance more than anything," he said. "One just has to put up with it."
There were sporadic flare-ups between strike organisers and police in other parts of the Basque region and Navarra, which is 25 percent Basque, and police detained nearly 100 people.

Trains and buses maintained regular service, escorted by police in most of the region, but there were some temporary interruptions due to road blockades and barricades on railway lines that were later cleared away.
Most schools were open, despite receiving bomb threats, and bigger businesses and factories operated normally, police said.

Spanish and Basque officials called the strike a "complete failure" while HB said it had been observed in many villages, city neighbourhoods and at universities, where students wanting to go to classes had to pass angry pickets.
"It's been a complete failure despite the fact that the call to strike was based on threats," a spokeswoman for the ruling conservatives in the Basque region told Reuters.
"The Basque society has behaved beautifully...showing a capacity to overcome the fear and blackmail of HB."
Businesses in some areas took collective decisions to open on Saturday instead of Friday to avoid pressure from the rebels, but others insisted they would not be blackmailed with violence.
HB sent threatening letters to businesses, schools and workers this week urging them to observe the work stoppage.
The letters sent a shiver of fear through Basque society, which has learned in 29 years of ETA's struggle for independence that the separatists do not make idle threats.
ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) has killed some 800 people, many of them for failing to cooperate with the group.

HB, which is supported by an estimated 10-15 percent of Basques, has planned demonstrations throughout the day saying its rights to meet, espouse a political point of view and to strike are being violated.
"There are many issues, but the main one today is to get our leaders freed," one protester said.
The Spanish Supreme Court has jailed 18 of HB's 25-member leadership in the past few weeks for failing to appear to answer charges they promoted violence.
The strike exacerbated tension in the region, already running high because ETA had stepped up its deadly attacks this year, killing six people including a Supreme Court judge.
A court verdict on the eve of the strike that freed the alleged killer of two policemen under Spain's fledgling jury system added to the feeling of outrage in the troubled region.
